Geography - Physical geography - Climatology.
Geography divides into physical and human geography, and climatology is one of the branches of physical geography.

Migration - International - India to Australia.
Movement across the boundary of a country is international migration, and a move from India to Australia is an example of it.

Formal region - Distinct boundaries - State.
A formal region is uniform in the chosen feature and has clear boundaries, and a state is a formal region bounded by administration.

Urban land use - Industrial area - Commercial area.
The land of a town is put to several uses at once, and the industrial and commercial areas are two of the recognised categories.

A rising dependency ratio means more children and elderly for every worker, which does strain the economy. It strains it partly because the elderly need costly medical care that the working group must pay for, so R explains A.

(A) Only A is correct.
As a city grows it takes on administration, trade, industry, education and transport together, so A is right. But a city rarely has only one function; most large cities are multifunctional, so R is wrong.

(D) Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Indian industry does produce a wide range of goods, and India is predominantly agrarian. But industrial diversity comes from the variety of raw materials, minerals, skills and markets, not from the fact that most people farm, so R does not explain A.

(C) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Population and regional development are indeed interrelated, and the reason is that the size, quality and skills of the population decide how far a region's resources can be used. So R explains A.

(A) Only A is correct.
A geographer today must know remote sensing, GIS, GPS and statistical software, so A is right. R is wrong, because computer applications are used in geography constantly, for mapping, analysis and planning.

(c) Relief.
Age structure, sex ratio and occupational structure are all ways of composing a population. Relief is a feature of the land, not of the people, so it is the incorrect factor.

(d) Regional settlement.
By the spacing of houses settlements are compact, dispersed or isolated. There is no type called a regional settlement, so it is the incorrect factor.

(a) Ancillary sector.
By ownership industries are of the public, private, joint and co-operative sectors. An ancillary industry is one that supplies parts to a larger industry, which is a classification by output, not by ownership.

(b) Language.
Literacy, life expectancy and the quality of population all measure how developed a region is. The language people speak says nothing about the level of development, so it is the incorrect factor.

(C) Shakespeare.
Hecataeus, Ptolemy and Strabo were scholars of the ancient world who wrote on geography. Shakespeare was a dramatist and poet, so he is the incorrect factor.

False.
Man lives, works and moves in groups, and settlements, languages, customs and institutions all arise from living together. Man is therefore a social animal.

Bread and other bakery goods are perishable and must reach the buyer fresh within hours, and they are bulky in relation to their value. Bakeries are therefore located close to the market, not away from it.

False.
Tertiary activities include the exchange of goods, that is trade and commerce, as well as services such as transport, banking, teaching and medicine. So they are not services alone.

A region is defined by the feature chosen and by the purpose in hand, so it may be as small as a city ward or as large as monsoon Asia.

Mountains have steep slopes on which farming and building are difficult, thin stony soil, severe cold, heavy snow and few routes. Little work is available and living is costly, so few people settle there and the population stays sparse.

Villages offer little work beyond farming, small and fragmented holdings, low wages and few schools and hospitals. Towns offer industry and service jobs, higher wages, education, medical care and entertainment. These push and pull factors together keep rural to urban migration increasing.

A large city becomes crowded and costly, and land inside it is scarce and dear. On its edge land is cheaper and more open, and improved roads and local trains let a person live there and still work in the city. So people and industries move outward and the suburbs develop rapidly.

In South America the Amazon forest and the Andes cover much of the continent, population is thin and scattered so both labour and market are small, capital and technology are short, and transport across forest and mountain is costly. For these reasons industrial growth has remained limited.

Air transport is by far the fastest means, it can cross mountains, deserts, forests and oceans where no road or rail can be built, and it is the only means for urgent goods, perishables and long distance passengers. As incomes, trade and tourism grow and fares fall, the use of airways keeps increasing.

An illiterate and poor population cannot take up skilled work, cannot use new technology and cannot save or invest, and it spends what it earns on bare necessities. The region's resources therefore remain unused and its productivity stays low, so illiteracy and poverty hold back regional development.

Triangular settlement: houses take the shape of a triangle, and this happens where two roads or two rivers meet at an angle, or at a confluence, so that the built up land is enclosed by three sides.
Circular settlement: houses stand in a ring, usually round a lake, a tank, a pond or a central open space used for cattle, with the fields lying outside the ring.

Expansive pyramid: very wide base and sharply narrowing top; shows a high birth rate and a high proportion of children, with few elderly; found in developing countries with a growing population, as in Nigeria and Bangladesh.
Constrictive pyramid: narrow base and comparatively broad middle and top; shows a falling birth rate, fewer children and a large proportion of adults and elderly; found in developed countries whose population is ageing, as in Japan and Germany.

Crude birth rate: the number of live births in a year per thousand of the population. It depends on fertility, on the age at marriage, on education and on family planning, and it raises the population.
Crude death rate: the number of deaths in a year per thousand of the population. It depends on medical care, nutrition, sanitation and the age structure, and it lowers the population. The difference between the two gives the natural growth rate.

Large-scale industries: very large capital, heavy machinery, hundreds or thousands of workers, mass production for a wide market, as in iron and steel, cement and automobiles.
Cottage industries: very small capital, simple tools worked by hand, the family itself as the labour force, work done at home, small output sold locally, as in handloom weaving, pottery, basket making and khadi.

Human geography: studies people and their activities - population, settlements, economic activities, society, politics and culture; its branches are population, settlement, economic, social, political and historical geography.
Physical geography: studies the natural environment - relief, climate, soil, water, plants and animals; its branches are geomorphology, climatology, hydrology, soil geography and biogeography.

Shifting agriculture is the oldest and simplest form of farming, practised in the tropical forests of Africa, South America, South-East Asia and North-East India.
A patch of forest is cleared with an axe and the felled trees are burnt, so it is also called slash and burn farming.
Mixed food crops such as maize, millet, yam, cassava and upland rice are sown on the ash with a hoe or a digging stick. No plough, manure, irrigation or machinery is used.
The ash keeps the soil fertile for only two or three years. When the yield falls the plot is abandoned, the forest is allowed to grow back on it, and a new patch is cleared.
Holdings are tiny, yields are low and the whole crop is eaten by the family, so it is a subsistence system.
It is known by local names - jhum in North-East India, milpa in Central America, ladang in Indonesia and chena in Sri Lanka.
It destroys forest and, where the population has grown and the fallow period has shortened, it leaves the soil exhausted and the slopes eroded.

By the source of their raw material industries are of four kinds.
Agro-based industries use the produce of farming, as in sugar, cotton textiles, edible oil, tea and tobacco.
Mineral based industries use minerals, as in iron and steel, cement, aluminium and petrochemicals.
Pastoral or animal based industries use the produce of animals, as in dairy, leather, woollen textiles and meat packing.
Forest based industries use the produce of forests, as in paper and pulp, plywood, furniture, lac and resin.
A marine based group is sometimes added for industries using the produce of the sea, such as fish canning.

Communication means carrying information, and it is different from transport, which carries goods and people.
Personal means carry a message to one named person - post, telegram, telephone, mobile and e-mail.
Mass means carry a message to many people at once - newspapers, radio, television and the internet.
Modern communication rests on satellites, optical fibre and mobile networks.
Its importance: it makes trade, banking and administration possible over any distance; it carries weather warnings and disaster alerts and so saves life; it spreads education and medical advice to remote areas through tele-education and telemedicine; it binds a country together and links it to the world; and by allowing work and meetings to be done from a distance it reduces the need to travel.

Regional imbalance means that some regions of India develop far faster than others.
Its causes are: an unfavourable physical setting, such as rugged relief in the hills, drought in the rain shadow and poor soil in the plateau; the uneven distribution of minerals and water; poor transport and power supply in the interior; low literacy, poor health and low skills; the concentration of industry and investment in a few already developed regions such as Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai, because investors go where infrastructure already exists; the historical neglect of some regions under colonial rule, when development followed the ports; and political and administrative neglect since.
The result is that people, industry and income concentrate in a few regions while others lose their young people to migration and fall further behind.

Geography today uses new tools and has opened new fields.
Remote sensing collects data about the earth from satellites without touching it. Geographical Information System stores, layers and analyses that data and makes maps to order. Global Positioning System gives the exact position of any point. Digital cartography has replaced hand drawn maps.
These have created new areas of work - disaster management, urban and regional planning, environmental impact assessment, watershed and land use planning, transport and market analysis, tourism and defence.
Geography has therefore become an applied and employable subject, and a geographer now works with computers and satellite images as much as with maps.

Human factors are those created by people themselves. They can gather population into a place the physical setting would not favour, and empty a place that it does.
Economic activity is the strongest. Wherever industry, mining, trade or plantation work offers wages, people gather. The Ruhr in Germany, the Damodar valley in India and Kimberley in South Africa are crowded because of coal, iron and diamonds, not because of their relief or climate.
Transport and communication decide whether a place can be reached and its produce sold. Population is dense along river valleys, coasts, railway lines and highways, and thin where there are no routes, as in the interior of the Amazon basin.
Urbanisation draws people continuously from village to town, because the town concentrates work, education, medical care and entertainment. Mumbai, Delhi, Tokyo and New York have grown in this way.
Political factors matter greatly. Peace, law and order and a settled government attract people and investment, while war and persecution empty a region, as in Syria. Government policy can create population where there was none, as Brazil did by building Brasilia and India by building Chandigarh.
Social and cultural factors work the same way. Religious centres such as Varanasi and Mecca hold large populations, and so do educational centres such as Pune and Oxford.
Technology allows people to live where they could not before, by irrigating deserts as in Israel and Rajasthan, by air conditioning, and by reclaiming land from the sea as in the Netherlands.
So the physical setting decides where people CAN live, and the human factors decide where they actually DO live.

A primary economic activity is one in which man obtains a product directly from nature, without changing its form. Nothing is manufactured; the product is only gathered, caught, grown or dug out. These are the oldest occupations of mankind and still employ the largest number of people in the developing world.
Their types are:
Hunting and gathering - the oldest of all, in which man lives on wild animals, fish, fruit, roots and honey. It survives only among a few tribes, such as the pygmies of the Congo basin, the Bushmen of the Kalahari and the Eskimos of the Arctic, and it is disappearing as forests are cleared and hunting is banned.
Animal husbandry - the rearing of animals for milk, meat, wool and hides. It is of two kinds: nomadic herding, practised in dry and cold lands where herders move with their animals in search of pasture, and commercial animal rearing, practised on large ranches in the temperate grasslands of the Prairies, Pampas, Veld and Downs with scientific breeding and machinery.
Fishing - the catching of fish from seas, rivers and lakes. It is concentrated on the continental shelves where warm and cold currents meet and plankton is abundant, as on the Grand Bank, the Dogger Bank and the seas off Japan and Peru.
Lumbering - the felling of trees for timber and pulp. It is commercial in the temperate coniferous forests of Canada, the U.S.A., Sweden, Finland and Russia, where the trees are softwood, straight and of one kind.
Mining - the taking out of minerals from the earth's crust. It may be open cast or underground, and it depends on geology, on the value of the mineral and on capital and technology, not on latitude.
Agriculture - the growing of crops, and the largest of all primary activities. It ranges from shifting and intensive subsistence farming to plantation, mixed, dairy and extensive commercial grain farming.
All of these are directly dependent on the natural environment, so they are strongly controlled by relief, climate, soil and the occurrence of resources.
